doc.title: 68088_Wilbur B. Ware, Sr oral history interview

chapter: Riverside and the New York scene
title: Musicians telling stories and the closeness lost in modern music
summary: Gloria raises Duke on messages between musicians; Ware talks about telling stories with music and the lost eye contact on big stages.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: But let me ask you this. Duke also talked about the messages that passed between musicians; he said the audience might not even be aware of it, but and this is early on, this is 20 years before what you were talking about -- people have messages between each other; they tell stories and have different things. There was one incident; he talked about, who was it, Sidney Bechet said, he was gonna call his a dog, but that's what he did. That's
the sound that he wanted to convey the message for.

Well, that was the music. You know that's what music is about, actually. You know, you're telling stories, you know, and you're painting pictures, and I can't explain it, but you hit it on the head; Duke hit it on the head. A lot of musicians know about that, just like we were playing when I was working with Flip as a youngster, musicians during that time were playing nightclubs, you were playing something and somebody might hit a sour note, a wrong note, and straining to reach it, and brush his shirt off like he's got some lint on it, and you get that hog out of there. He's cutting th e holes. But music is beautiful. It always will be, you know.

I was always partial to the blues (acoustic) ... but nowadays everything is so technical; you know, it seems like they don't want you to look at each other when you're playing, usually, unless you're up on a big concert stage, you know, when you're 25 feet away from each other, there is no closeness there.
